title: Module 1: Foundations of Money and Investing

submodules.title: 1. The Basics of Money and Finance
submodules.intro: Is keeping money the same as growing money?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: SAVING VS. INVESTING
Saving: keeping money aside for future use. It is generally safer and easier to access.
Investing: putting money into assets that may grow in value or generate income. Returns are not guaranteed.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: INFLATION
Inflation means the general prices of goods and services rise over time, so the same money buys fewer things.
Today: ₹100 buys a sandwich (₹50) and a juice (₹50). A few years later, both cost more and ₹100 may not be enough.
Your money hasn't disappeared, but its purchasing power has decreased.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: TIME VALUE OF MONEY
Money today is generally worth more than the same amount later, because today's money can be saved or invested to earn returns.
Choice A: ₹1,000 today. Choice B: ₹1,000 after three years. Choice A lets you save or invest in the meantime.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Saving protects money for planned needs; investing aims to grow it, with risk.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between saving and investing?
options: Saving keeps money aside, while investing aims to grow it
quiz.explanation: Saving keeps money aside; investing aims for growth but returns are not guaranteed.

quiz.question: What happens to the purchasing power of money when inflation increases?
quiz.explanation: Rising prices mean the same money buys less.

quiz.question: Why can receiving money today be more valuable than the same amount later?
options: Today's money can be saved or invested to earn returns
quiz.explanation: Money today can start earning returns right away.

submodules.title: 2. The Power of Compounding
submodules.intro: Can your money make more money?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: COMPOUNDING
Compounding happens when your returns start earning returns of their own. You earn on your original money, and then on the growth as well.
Example (hypothetical): ₹1,000 at 10% a year becomes ₹1,331 after 3 years. This is a mathematical example, not a promised return.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE RULE OF 72
Years to double = 72 ÷ Annual return (%)
• 6% return → about 12 years
• 8% return → about 9 years
• 12% return → about 6 years

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: EARLY VS. LATE
Aarav starts at age 20 and Rohan at age 30. Both invest a hypothetical ₹10,000 once at an assumed 8% a year.
• Aarav (20 years) → about ₹46,610 at age 40
• Rohan (10 years) → about ₹21,589 at age 40

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Time can make a significant difference to compound growth.

quiz.question: What makes compounding different from simple interest?
options: Returns earn returns of their own
quiz.explanation: Compounding earns returns on both the original money and previous growth.

quiz.question: What does the Rule of 72 help estimate?
options: How long money takes to double

quiz.question: At an 8% annual return, roughly how long to double money?
Why does starting early make a difference?
options: More time for returns to compound
quiz.explanation: More time lets growth build on growth.

submodules.title: 3. Understanding Asset Classes
submodules.intro: Where do people put their money?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: THE FIVE ASSET CLASSES
An asset class is a group of investments that share similar characteristics.

1. Equity (Stocks): owning a small part of a company. Value can rise or fall. Higher risk generally.

2. Debt: lending money to a government or company through instruments like bonds. The borrower agrees to repay on specified terms. Generally lower risk than equity, depending on the issuer.

3. Gold: a precious metal held as a store of value or for diversification (coins, gold ETFs). Its price can fluctuate.

4. Real Estate: houses, apartments or commercial buildings. Can be expensive and hard to sell quickly.

5. Cash and Cash Equivalents: cash, savings accounts and short-term instruments. Easy to access, but inflation can reduce purchasing power.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Each asset class has its own mix of risk, return and ease of access.

options: Owning a small part of a company

submodules.title: 4. Understanding Risk and Return
submodules.intro: Why can you earn more but also lose more?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: RISK AND RETURN
Risk: the possibility that an investment may not perform as expected, including losing money.
Return: money gained or lost over a period, usually as a percentage.
Example: ₹1,000 rises to ₹1,200 → gain of ₹200 (20%). Falls to ₹800 → loss of ₹200 (20%).

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
Higher potential returns generally come with higher risk. This does NOT mean higher risk guarantees higher returns.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: TYPES OF RISK
• Market Risk: overall market prices fall.
• Business Risk: a company faces difficulties, e.g. falling sales.
• Inflation Risk: money loses purchasing power.
• Liquidity Risk: difficulty selling an asset quickly.
• Interest Rate Risk: changing rates affect investment values, e.g. bond prices.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: RISK APPETITE
Risk appetite is how much risk someone is comfortable taking and can financially afford. Aarav prefers stability and needs money soon; Ishaan has a longer goal and accepts fluctuations. Neither is automatically right.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
The best decision suits your goal, time horizon and ability to handle risk. (Educational only, not a financial risk assessment.)

quiz.question: Does higher risk guarantee higher returns?
options: No, it only means greater possible gains and losses
quiz.explanation: Risk raises the range of outcomes, not the guarantee.

quiz.question: Difficulty selling a property quickly is which risk?
Why consider your goal before choosing an investment?
options: Goals decide time horizon and how much risk fits
quiz.explanation: The right investment depends on goal, horizon and risk capacity.

submodules.title: 5. Setting Financial Goals
submodules.intro: How do you turn a money dream into a money plan?
submodules.content:
⚡ MISSION BRIEFING: THREE TYPES OF GOALS
• Short-term: usually within 1 year (e.g. ₹3,000 for headphones).
• Medium-term: around 1-5 years (e.g. a laptop or future education expense).
• Long-term: more than 5 years (e.g. higher education, long-term financial security).
These are learning categories, not fixed rules.

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: THE SMART METHOD
• S - Specific: buy a laptop
• M - Measurable: save ₹30,000
• A - Achievable: save an affordable amount regularly
• R - Relevant: needed for studies
• T - Time-bound: within 12 months

⚡ FINANCIAL INTEL: MATCHING GOALS WITH TIME
• Need money soon? Prioritise safety and easy access.
• More time? You can learn about investment options and their risks.
• Long-term goal? Understand how inflation and compounding affect the amount needed.

🍕 CASE STUDY: THE LAPTOP CHALLENGE
Riya wants a ₹30,000 laptop in 12 months and has ₹6,000 saved. Remaining ₹24,000 ÷ 12 months = ₹2,000 per month.

💡 CORE TAKEAWAY:
SEBI suggests considering goals, risk appetite and investment horizon together.

quiz.question: Riya needs ₹24,000 more in 12 months. Monthly saving?
For a goal needed soon, what should be prioritised?
quiz.explanation: Short horizons favour safety and liquidity.
